meta.title: Who really said "The American Republic will endure until the day Congress discovers that it can bribe the public with the public's money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Tocqueville, and not Alexander Fraser Tytler either. The sentiment first appears in print in an Oklahoma newspaper column of December 1951 — 92 years after Tocqueville died.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The American Republic will endure until the day Congress discovers that it can bribe the public with the public's money'?
meta.ogDescription: A staple of budget speeches that neither of its two credited authors wrote. The earliest known appearance is a 1951 Daily Oklahoman op-ed, which pinned it on a Scot dead since 1813.

answer.label: Not Tocqueville — and not Tytler
answer.authorDates: Unattributed · the sentiment first known in print, December 1951
answer.sourceLine: This is not in Democracy in America and not anywhere else in Tocqueville; Wikiquote files it under Misattributed the entry ↗. It is a variant of a passage usually credited either to Tocqueville or to the Scottish judge Alexander Fraser Tytler, and the earliest known appearance of that passage is an unsourced attribution to Tytler in Elmer T. Peterson’s column ‘This is the Hard Core of Freedom’, The Daily Oklahoman, 9 December 1951 Wikipedia’s account ↗. Tocqueville died in 1859; Tytler died in 1813. Neither wrote a line first recorded in 1951, and there is no reliable record of Tytler writing any part of it.

source.heading: The source — a 1951 newspaper column

docMeta.dd: Elmer T. Peterson, The Daily Oklahoman, 9 December 1951, p. 12A

source.excerpt: A democracy cannot exist as a permanent form of government. It can only exist until the majority discovers it can vote itself largess out of the public treasury. After that, the majority always votes for the candidate promising the most benefits with the result the democracy collapses because of the loose fiscal policy ensuing, always to be followed by a dictatorship, then a monarchy.
trail: Wikiquote calls it misattributed and names the origin. Its Tocqueville entry describes the line as ‘a variant expression of a sentiment which is often attributed to Tocqueville or Alexander Fraser Tytler’, and gives the earliest known occurrence as the unsourced Tytler attribution in Peterson’s 1951 column the entry ↗. We take that finding as it stands and claim nothing earlier.

Wikipedia’s Tytler article reaches the same place independently. It reproduces the 1951 Daily Oklahoman paragraph, cites it to p. 12A, and states flatly that there is no reliable record of Tytler having written any part of the text — adding that the passage and the better-known ‘from bondage to spiritual faith’ cycle did not even appear together until the 1970s Debatable attribution ↗.
It is not in the book. The searchable Reeve translation of Democracy in America has no ‘largess’, no ‘will endure until’, and no passage resembling this prophecy at all volume one ↗ volume two ↗.
The dates rule both men out. Tocqueville lived 1805–1859 his life ↗; Tytler lived 1747–1813 his life ↗. A sentence whose earliest known appearance is December 1951 cannot be the work of either.
source.cutTag: Elmer T. Peterson, The Daily Oklahoman, 9 December 1951
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote on this page either. It is the passage the quote is a compression of — the earliest known form of the idea, as Peterson printed it in 1951 above the words ‘Two centuries ago, a somewhat obscure Scotsman named Tytler made this profound observation’. He gave no source, and none has ever been found. The Tocqueville version, with Congress and the public’s money, is a later rewrite of it.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Tocqueville
author.metaLine: 1805–1859 · French diplomat, political philosopher and historian
author.bio: Alexis de Tocqueville did write, at length and in earnest, about the dangers democracies pose to themselves — the tyranny of the majority, the soft despotism of a benevolent state. That is precisely why this line sticks to him: it sounds like a compression of something he might have argued, which is the most durable kind of fake. But he wrote in the 1830s, about a federal government that did almost nothing, and the specific mechanism here — a legislature buying votes with the electorate’s own tax money — is a mid-twentieth-century American anxiety in mid-twentieth-century American phrasing. The other name attached to it, the Edinburgh judge Alexander Fraser Tytler, fits no better: he died in 1813.

misattribution.heading: Two false credits, neither with a source
misattribution.intro: A saying credited to two different men who died 46 years apart, neither of whom left a trace of it, and whose earliest known appearance is an op-ed in an Oklahoma newspaper in the winter of 1951.

items.why: Absent from Democracy in America and from the rest of his work; Wikiquote lists it as misattributed the entry ↗. He died in 1859 his life ↗.

Peterson’s 1951 column introduced the passage as the observation of ‘a somewhat obscure Scotsman named Tytler’ and gave no source. Wikipedia states there is no reliable record of Tytler having written any part of the text Debatable attribution ↗. Tytler died in 1813.

The 1951 Daily Oklahoman column ‘This is the Hard Core of Freedom’ is the earliest known appearance of the passage, not a claim that Peterson invented it — he presented it as a quotation. Where he got it is unknown the citation ↗.

The list running from bondage to spiritual faith to liberty and back to bondage is usually quoted alongside this passage as though both were Tytler’s. It is a different text with a different history — first known in a 1943 speech by Henning W. Prentis, Jr. — and the two did not begin appearing together until the 1970s the account ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote it. The idea’s earliest known appearance is an unsourced attribution to Tytler in The Daily Oklahoman of 9 December 1951; Tocqueville had been dead for ninety-two years the earliest known occurrence ↗.

context.heading: Why it keeps getting quoted
lead: It is one of the most-cited lines in American fiscal politics, and its appeal is that it converts a contested political argument into a settled historical prophecy. Attach a nineteenth-century French aristocrat to it and a claim about spending stops being your opinion and becomes something foretold.

That is also why the 1951 date matters more than the usual pedantry about sourcing. The line is not an old warning that America failed to heed; it is a piece of mid-century American commentary that acquired a nineteenth-century pedigree because the pedigree made it harder to argue with.
detailsBody: 1813: Alexander Fraser Tytler dies, having written nothing resembling the passage.
1859: Tocqueville dies. Democracy in America contains no version of it.
February 1943: Henning W. Prentis, Jr. delivers the ‘from bondage to spiritual faith’ cycle in a speech at the University of Pennsylvania — a separate text often quoted alongside this one.

9 December 1951: Elmer T. Peterson prints the ‘vote itself largess out of the public treasury’ paragraph in The Daily Oklahoman, crediting Tytler and citing nothing. This is the earliest known appearance.
1970s: the two passages begin to circulate as a single quotation.
Later: the Congress-and-the-public’s-money rewrite appears and migrates to Tocqueville, whose name carries more weight with an American audience than an obscure Scottish judge’s.
context.pull: It is not a prophecy from 1835. It is a newspaper column from 1951 wearing a wig.
